column1: Why can no header, patch, or WAF rule fully eliminate the web's structural security vulnerabilities?
column2: Because HTTP's original design (1991) was built for document sharing, not security; trust boundaries are protocol agreements between components that cannot cryptographically verify each other's internal state, unlike a hardware root of trust (TPM/TrustZone).

column1: In the web-specific CIA triad, what distinguishes an Integrity violation from a Confidentiality violation?
column2: Confidentiality concerns data crossing trust boundaries without authorization (e.g., CORS misconfig leaking data); Integrity concerns whether a resource/request is unmodified and authorized by the legitimate principal — e.g., CSRF causes a valid authenticated request to execute an unsanctioned state change.

column1: What is the single root cause shared by all injection vulnerability classes (SQL, shell, template, XSS)?
column2: A system accepts data from an untrusted source and passes it, without transformation, into a context where it is interpreted as instructions rather than values — breaking channel separation between control tokens and data tokens.

column1: What is the 'channel separation' invariant in injection vulnerabilities?
column2: Every interpreter's token stream consists of control tokens (keywords, metacharacters) and data tokens (literals); a secure system ensures attacker-controlled bytes never reach the control token position in the parse tree.

column1: Why does string interpolation in SQL query construction create a structural (not edge-case) vulnerability?
column2: Because concatenated strings build the parse tree at runtime without enforcing a data/control boundary at the syntax level — if an attacker's string literal produces a token classified as a keyword/operator, the parse tree's shape changes and the DB executes a different query than the developer intended.

column1: What is the core security invariant of session management stated in Lesson 3?
column2: 'The token is the identity' — the session token is a bearer credential; whoever holds it authenticates as the user. Compromising the token requires neither the password nor breaking the hash function, only extracting or predicting the token.

column1: Why is storing plain SHA-256 password hashes catastrophically vulnerable despite not being plaintext?
column2: SHA-256 is optimized for throughput (GPUs compute hundreds of billions of ops/sec), enabling precomputation via rainbow tables and fast offline dictionary attacks, cracking most real-world passwords within hours.

column1: What two components make password hashing resistant to precomputation and brute force, and what does each defeat?
column2: Salt (unique random value per credential) defeats precomputed rainbow tables; Work factor (deliberately slowed computation) defeats brute-force/dictionary throughput attacks.

column1: What is the Dolev-Yao threat model, and why is it the foundational assumption underlying TLS design?
column2: It assumes the adversary has complete control of the network — able to intercept, replay, modify, or inject any message in transit. TLS's core invariant is that even under this full network compromise, no adversary should recover plaintext or forge a valid connection to a legitimate origin, provided certificate validation and crypto primitives hold.

column1: What critical caveat undermines the TLS security invariant in practice, as shown by BEAST, POODLE, DROWN, and Heartbleed?
column2: The invariant only holds if validation is done 'correctly.' These vulnerabilities arose from implementation flaws, protocol version weaknesses, and downgrade paths — the spec can be sound while the implementation (spanning millions of lines of C code) is catastrophically broken.

column1: What distinct trust boundary does the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) enforce, as opposed to transport-layer trust (TLS)?
column2: SOP enforces origin-level trust: boundaries between documents from different sources so that a script from one origin (e.g., evil.com) cannot read data/cookies belonging to another origin (e.g., bank.com), independent of whether the transport channel itself is secure.

column1: How can application-layer Availability attacks succeed using traffic volumes well within normal envelopes?
column2: By targeting resource-asymmetric endpoints — e.g., an unauthenticated API triggering an expensive database query, or input causing a regex engine to undergo catastrophic backtracking — exhausting server resources without needing volumetric DDoS-scale traffic.
